Kevin O’Leary is pulling back. The investor and Shark Tank personality nicknamed “Mr. Wonderful” has agreed to nearly halve his proposed Stratos AI data center in Utah, trimming it from 40,000 acres to around 19,430, following intense community opposition and mounting pressure from state legislators.

The rollback came in response to Utah Senate President Stuart Adams, who publicly demanded a 75% reduction to roughly 10,000 acres. Adams also called for concrete water conservation measures, greater project transparency, and meaningful protections for wildlife, agricultural land, and the Great Salt Lake.

O’Leary made no effort to spin it. “I have no choice,” he told NBC News, a straightforward admission that public and political resistance had cornered him.

The sticking point: O’Leary’s concession only goes halfway, literally. The downsized project would still span more land than many American cities, and the residents who have been pushing back for months aren’t satisfied. As far as they’re concerned, half of something enormous is still enormous.

At its original scale, Stratos would have been one of the most expansive AI data centers ever built, placing heavy demands on land, water, and energy in a state that can’t afford to spare much of any of them. The central question now is whether cutting the project in half is enough to win over the ranchers, families, and lawmakers who made clear they weren’t going to accept it quietly. See less

BOX ELDER COUNTY, Utah — Kevin O’Leary, the celebrity investor and brash “Shark Tank” TV pitchman, wanted land, and lots of it, for his next big deal — building one of the world’s largest data centers.

The Stratos Hyperscale Data Center, a massive, controversial development proposed by "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary in Box Elder County, Utah.  

​The story behind it involves significant scale, environmental concerns, and a public backlash:
​Immense Scope: Initially, the project was envisioned to span 40,000 acres, which was frequently described as being twice the size of Manhattan. O'Leary later clarified that the actual data center facility would cover 10,000 acres within that larger site.  

​Power and Energy: The facility was designed to generate up to 9 gigawatts of power—more than double the current electricity consumption of the entire state of Utah—using proprietary natural gas power plants. Critics pointed out that this could significantly increase Utah's greenhouse gas emissions and generate massive amounts of waste heat.  

​Public Backlash: Residents and environmental groups expressed strong concerns regarding the project's environmental impact, particularly its potential effect on the Great Salt Lake, local air quality, and the desert ecosystem.  

​Scaling Back: Following intense public pressure and requests from Utah lawmakers to reduce the project's footprint, O'Leary agreed to scale back the development. In 2026, he committed to removing nearly 20,000 acres from the project, effectively downsizing the industrial footprint.  

​O'Leary's Stance: O'Leary has acknowledged that he and his partners "screwed up" the initial rollout by failing to be transparent with the local community, but he remains committed to the project, arguing that the global race for AI dominance makes such massive infrastructure necessary for U.S. productivity. ✝️🐑

"Shark Tank" star Kevin O'Leary is officially scaling back his controversial AI data center in Utah after facing massive community backlash!

O'Leary's proposed "Stratos" project was originally slated to be a staggering 40,000-acre AI data center—one of the largest on Earth. However, the massive footprint drew intense outrage from local residents and state lawmakers concerned about the massive drain on land, water, and power in the drought-prone state.

Utah Senate President Stuart Adams publicly demanded O'Leary shrink the project by 75% and commit to stronger environmental protections for local farmland, wildlife, and the Great Salt Lake.

Sensing the mounting pressure, "Mr. Wonderful" admitted he had "no choice" and agreed to cut the project's size. But here is the catch: he is only shrinking it by roughly half—down to about 19,430 acres—not the 75% lawmakers originally requested.

While the reduction is a significant step, the revised plan still covers an area larger than many American cities. Now, local families, ranchers, and environmentalists who fought the project are left wondering if half a giant is still a giant.

A group of Utah residents just decided they're done being ignored — and they're taking the fight to court.

The Alliance for a Better Utah and five Box Elder County residents filed suit Wednesday in Utah's 3rd District Court over the approval of Kevin O'Leary's "Stratos Project" — a sprawling AI data center planned for the rural Hansel Valley. Their core argument is simple but explosive: the people who actually live there were never given a real say.

The lawsuit targets the Military Installation Development Authority, or MIDA — an unelected body that signed off on the project. Plaintiffs say MIDA exercised powers "the Utah Constitution never authorized," approving a development that could reshape residents' water, land, environment, and daily lives without any democratic vote. It also names the Box Elder County Commission, Senate President J. Stuart Adams, and state Sen. Jerry Stevenson.

Here's the part raising eyebrows: Adams and Stevenson are sitting legislators who also serve on the MIDA board. The suit argues that holding both roles may violate Utah's ban on occupying more than one office of public trust at once — and that it should render the project's approval null and void.

The pressure is already working. O'Leary has conceded to shrinking the original 40,000-acre footprint by roughly 75%, committing water to the shrinking Great Salt Lake, and setting aside thousands of acres for open space, wildlife, and farming. But the plaintiffs want the court to throw out the approval entirely and permanently block the plan.

The question now: can a handful of residents stop a billionaire's data center empire — and force their own government to answer for how it got approved?

Kevin O'Leary is backing down. The Shark Tank investor known as "Mr. Wonderful" has agreed to cut his planned Stratos AI data center in Utah by roughly half — shrinking it from a staggering 40,000 acres to about 19,430 acres — after a wave of local outrage and pressure from state lawmakers.

The retreat came after Utah Senate President Stuart Adams publicly demanded the project shrink by 75%, down to around 10,000 acres. Adams didn't stop there. He also pushed for stronger water conservation, real transparency, and protections for wildlife habitat, farmland, and the Great Salt Lake.

O'Leary's response was blunt. "I have no choice," he told NBC News, signaling that the political and community backlash had left him little room to maneuver.

But here's the catch: O'Leary is only cutting about half — not the 75% lawmakers asked for. The revised plan would still cover an area larger than many American cities, and residents who have spent months fighting the project say half a giant is still a giant.

The Stratos project would have been one of the largest AI data centers on Earth, devouring enormous amounts of land, water, and power in a drought-prone state. Now the question is whether "roughly half" is enough to satisfy the families, ranchers, and lawmakers who refused to stay quiet.

O’Leary’s announcement is the latest development in a fight playing out between Utah politicians and the Canadian businessman. A proposed 40,000-acre data center campus in northern Utah is drawing increasing attention from state leaders and local residents as concerns grow over its size, resource demands, and potential environmental impact.

The project, backed by investor Kevin O’Leary, would be built near the Great Salt Lake, a region already facing long-term environmental challenges. In response to public concerns, Utah Senate President Stuart Adams announced that he has formally requested a significant reduction in the project's footprint.

In a statement released Monday, Adams said he sent a letter to O’Leary calling for the proposed development area to be reduced by 75%, from 40,000 acres to approximately 10,000 acres. He also stated that any excess water associated with the project should be treated and dedicated to supporting the Great Salt Lake.

Adams, who serves on the board of the Military Installation Development Authority (MIDA) — the agency overseeing the project in Box Elder County — said additional safeguards are needed as the development moves through the review process.

The proposal has generated widespread public discussion in recent weeks, with critics raising concerns about water consumption, energy use, emissions, and the overall scale of the project. Supporters, meanwhile, point to the potential economic benefits and technological investment it could bring to the region.

Adams also called for greater transparency, stronger conservation measures, and enhanced protections for Utah’s natural resources.

“Utah can pursue economic opportunity while protecting our water, air, wildlife, and communities,” Adams said. “We can and must do both.”

The project remains under review as state officials, developers, and community members continue to debate its future and potential impact on the region.

More than 600 people packed the Utah State Capitol this week to push back against a proposed data center the size of a small city — and they say the Great Salt Lake could pay the price.

The project, known as "Wonder Valley" (also called Stratos), would span roughly 40,000 acres in Box Elder County. It's backed by "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary, who has pitched it as a major economic engine that could bring jobs, infrastructure, and billions in investment to northern Utah.

But the residents who rallied at the Capitol have one overriding concern: water. Data centers consume enormous amounts of it for cooling, and the Great Salt Lake has already been shrinking for years. Opponents fear a development this large could draw down the water supply even further and accelerate the lake's decline — a problem that affects air quality, wildlife, and the regional economy.

Supporters of the project argue it could be designed with water-efficient cooling and would deliver long-term economic benefits to a rural part of the state. Backers also point to growing demand for computing power and the chance for Utah to become a hub for it.

More than 600 people packed the Utah State Capitol this weekend, and their message was simple: hands off our water.

They came out to oppose a massive data center backed by Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary - the TV personality known as "Mr. Wonderful." The project, officially called "Stratos" but nicknamed "Wonder Valley," would sprawl across more than 40,000 acres of Box Elder County in northern Utah. It was the second rally at the Capitol in under two weeks.

What's driving the anger? Water. The proposed site sits in a region tied directly to the health of the Great Salt Lake, which has been shrinking for years. Protesters warn the facility could pull even more water from an already depleted lake. They also point to projections that the project could more than double Utah's electricity use and significantly raise the state's carbon footprint, with much of the power coming from natural gas.

O'Leary hasn't backed down. He claimed - without offering evidence - that the vast majority of the opponents were "bused in" from out of state and dismissed many as paid protesters. Residents pushed back hard, saying they're locals who simply don't want a private mega-project deciding the fate of their water and air.

The fight has scrambled the usual political lines. This isn't left versus right - it's people who live near the Great Salt Lake asking whether any one investor, no matter how rich, should be able to reshape an entire region's water supply. Supporters say the data center could bring jobs and investment. Opponents say no amount of money is worth gambling a dying lake.

Where do you land - is a project this big worth the risk to the Great Salt Lake?

Hundreds of Utahns descended on the state capitol on May 23rd with a blunt message: Kevin O'Leary's massive data center project is not welcome near the Great Salt Lake. The crowd chanted "data center dollars don't trickle down, Kevin O'Leary get out of our town" as speakers warned about what could happen to one of America's most fragile ecosystems if the project moves forward.

The project — called the Stratos Hyperscale Data Center — is a proposed 40,000-acre AI data center campus in Box Elder County, right along the northern shore of the Great Salt Lake. Backed by the Shark Tank investor, the facility would eventually demand 9 gigawatts of power — and experts say it could raise Utah's total carbon emissions by 64 percent once fully built. It's also expected to cost more than $100 billion when complete.

Box Elder County commissioners gave it the green light on May 4th. That approval lit the fuse. Grassroots groups formed almost overnight — including BEAR, the Box Elder Accountability Referendum, which is now pushing to let voters decide the project's fate directly. They argue county commissioners had no business making a decision this big behind closed doors.

The water question is the flashpoint. Critics say the project threatens to pull water from sources that feed the Great Salt Lake — a body of water that has already been shrinking for years. Developers insist they've designed a closed-loop system to recirculate water and protect the aquifer. But residents aren't buying it, and a second water rights application tied to the project was just withdrawn days after being filed.

O'Leary, for his part, has dismissed the protesters as paid professionals bused in from out of state and claimed critics are tied to the Chinese Communist Party. The EPA administrator visited the Great Salt Lake the very next day — and threw his support behind protecting it, while punting on the data center question directly.

Claims that we’re going to consume all of Utah’s electricity, drain the Great Salt Lake, or immediately build the world’s largest facility simply aren’t true. In fact, the goal is to eventually contribute power back into the local system to help stabilize energy costs.

This project would create thousands of construction jobs, thousands more long term engineering and support jobs, and major tax revenue for Box Elder County over the next decade. We’re also going through every required process EPA approvals, water permits, air permits, noise compliance, and public review.
